idiom_name: gRPC-Java generated OrderServiceImplBase + newStub(channel) with protobuf messages
implementation_notes: protoc with the Java plugin generates the service descriptor, an abstract ImplBase for the server and a newStub(channel) client, so the facade is the class implementing coarse methods (overriding the StreamObserver-based signatures) that delegate to the service layer, with protobuf messages as the transfer objects. The JDK-native alternative is RMI: the facade implements an interface extending java.rmi.Remote, declares RemoteException on every method and lets RMI's object serialisation ship the payloads by value through the registry. Choose plain RMI for a closed JVM-to-JVM boundary with no schema tooling; choose gRPC when more than one language, streaming or an HTTP/2 gateway is involved.
pitfalls: gRPC service implementations are invoked on multiple threads; the facade must be stateless or synchronise its state.
Do not block a gRPC event-loop thread with JDBC or other blocking I/O - offload server work to an executor and use the blocking stub only on the client.
The .proto is the API version contract: changing a field number or type silently breaks wire compatibility with already-deployed peers.

variants.name: RMI remote interface with Serializable payloads (classic)
variants.idiom_name: java.rmi.Remote remote interface + UnicastRemoteObject implementation + registry lookup
variants.implementation_notes: The classic JVM form: the facade implements an interface that extends java.rmi.Remote, every method declares throws RemoteException, and the client obtains a stub from the RMI registry (LocateRegistry/Naming.lookup); arguments and results are transferred by value, so the transfer objects must implement Serializable. It remains the shortest path for a JVM-only boundary with no IDL, but it exposes Java types on both sides and offers no cross-language story; RMI Activation was removed in JDK 17, so only plain RMI (registry plus stubs) should be used.
pitfalls: Every remote method declares RemoteException and callers must treat it as a first-class failure mode: a dead registry or server surfaces as an unchecked connection failure.
Serialisation is the wire format: adding a field is compatible, but changing a type or a serialVersionUID breaks deployed peers in confusing ways.
Returning another Remote object hands the client a new proxy and reintroduces chatty remote calls; return transfer objects instead.
